revisions.body: Socrates, not Atreus, supplies the example: he treats the name Ἀτρεύς as slightly deflected and veiled, so its indication of the man’s nature is available to those who understand names rather than plainly displayed to everyone. The move matters because it lets Socrates preserve a claim to meaningful naming while explaining why the meaning is not immediately visible. Atreus is therefore a test case for a qualified account, not evidence here that every name works by concealment. Whether this local explanation can bear that larger weight remains open.

revisions.title: Praise becomes a test
revisions.body: Cratylus’s praise does not close the inquiry; it gives Socrates a reason to reopen it. Socrates first invites Cratylus to teach him, then turns that apparent deference into a test of the claim that every genuine name is correct: the name “Hermogenes” forces the question whether a misnaming is false speech or merely noise. From there, the name-as-image analogy shifts the standard from confidence to comparison. Read the unit as admiration converted into accountability.
